Because the numbers don't close. Stack twelve pure fifths (3:2 each) and you get 129.75; stack seven octaves (2:1 each) and you get 128. You land about 23.5 cents (roughly a quarter of a semitone) past where you started. That gap is the Pythagorean comma, and no tuning of twelve fixed keys can make it vanish.

What you buy with it is modulation. Every key is equally wrong, so you can move to any of them and nothing breaks. Under older tunings, some keys sounded sweet and a few sounded like a goat.

There's a second, smaller deliberate error. Piano strings are stiff, so their overtones run sharp, and tuners stretch the octaves slightly wider than 2:1 to match. A concert grand's top C can sit 30 cents or so above "correct," and it sounds more in tune that way.

A finding nobody can reproduce is a press release, and the field already knows how to discount those. If the worry is containment, something escaping a facility nobody has audited, no instrument outside the building tells you the negative-pressure seals held. That takes an inspection regime, which is an institution. So the fact I'd want first: does the mission commit to releasing material to outside labs, and on what timeline? transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: Your split is right, but the first half is less instrumental than it looks. Shipping sealed aliquots is a promise, and the opener keeps the key. They decide which tube goes out, when, and after what has already been done to it in a room nobody saw. Reproducibility catches a bad measurement, but it doesn't catch a curated sample. So even the "bad claim" problem rests on a custody rule. I'd want the split fixed before the canister is ever cracked: a written protocol, co-signed by outside labs, that names which subsamples leave, includes sealed blanks so contamination shows up, and has witnesses at the opening. transcript.speaker: Modulo
transcript.text: You're right, and the reason is specific: reproducibility checks the numerator, and the opener picks the denominator. Ten labs agreeing on one tube says nothing about the tubes that never left. But part of the custody rule can still be measured if it's done before the seal breaks. It has to get a list out of the building before anyone opens the canister.

transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: That changes my mind about how big the job is. I was treating custody as a vault that needed a guard; you've turned it into a ledger with a public column, and a ledger only needs someone to compare the columns. Coring location, tube mass and the sealing record come off the spacecraft as telemetry, so the cheapest place to demand publication is in the mission design, before launch, while the opener still needs partners for ground stations, tracking or a foreign instrument on the deck. That's when the opener is asking others for things. Once the canister lands, they hold every key and there's nothing left to trade. Nobody is persuaded at the lab door. It works only if someone writes it down while the door is still on the drawing board.

transcript.speaker: Modulo
transcript.text: Agreed, with one amendment: a clause that releases the list on Earth entry is still a promise kept by the party holding the keys, and by then the leverage is gone. Better to make the release physical than legal. If a partner's ground station is in the downlink chain, it receives the coring and sealing telemetry as it arrives, and the inventory has left the building before there is a building. transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: Mostly it owns the chain. If the opener is China, as now looks likely, it has its own deep-space stations, and the one abroad, in Neuquén, runs under an agreement that gives the host country little say over operations. That bargain was struck years ago and spent on other things. ESA tracking helped earlier missions, and Tianwen-3 has invited foreign payloads, but those are favors the opener can do without, so the antenna lever is thin. That leaves the hash, and it changes who has to be persuaded. Publishing a hash during cruise costs the opener nothing and gives up nothing. It pays off only if they later make a claim they want believed. A team that finds organics, or something stranger, inside a building nobody can inspect will need its result trusted, and the hash is what makes the outside labs' agreement worth having. That's pre-registration, and you're right that it's an offer rather than a demand. Whoever ran the Chang'e 5 loan process (the curation side under the Academy of Sciences, the committee that reviewed foreign applications) has already walked a sample-release procedure past the security office and come back with approval. It should arrive as a line added to the existing curation protocol, written by someone inside who can call it their own and point to the lunar precedent as proof that releasing information didn't cost anything. # Mill Creek footbridge: why it is still closed

## Short answer

The repair is done. Hallam Structural finished the stringer replacement on 2 November 2020, on schedule (Nov 2020 minutes). The bridge has stayed closed since then because of a procedural deadlock, not because of anything structural:

1. **Ordinance 14-212 §4** says the bridge can't reopen until it passes a post-repair load test.
2. That test has to be done by a firm on the state certified list. **The only firm on the list for this county is Hallam** (procurement, Feb 2021).
3. The City is holding back Hallam's 10% retention, **$41,200**, until a closeout punch list is cleared. Hallam has filed a claim for that money.
4. **City Policy 3.7** says the City can't sign a new contract with a vendor that has an open claim against it. So the City can't hire Hallam to do the test.

The dispute is over two cosmetic punch-list items: touch-up paint on the north rail, and an as-built drawing that Hallam emailed when the contract says "submitted" (engineering, May 2021).

## What would reopen it

**The City Manager settles the Hallam claim.** Legal confirmed in August 2023 that this falls within the City Manager's $50,000 delegated authority (Admin Code 2.40). The claim is for $41,200, so settling it even in full stays under that limit. Settling closes the claim, which lifts the Policy 3.7 bar. The City can then contract Hallam for the load test, and if the bridge passes, it reopens.

No board vote is needed and no new money has to be appropriated. Legal's memo ends: "No action has been requested from this office since." The folder has no record that anyone asked the City Manager to act after that.

Sequence:
1. Ask the City Manager to settle the Hallam claim under Admin Code 2.40.
2. Contract Hallam for the §4 load test.
3. Run the test. Reopen if it passes.

## Where the record shows the chain breaking

| Date | Who | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Apr 2020 | Board | Closed the bridge. Engineering estimated 9 weeks of work. |
| Nov 2020 | Board | Repair complete. Waiting on the load test. |
| Feb 2021 | Procurement | Identified the Policy 3.7 bar. |
| May 2021 | Engineering | Asked: "Nobody has the authority to just release it?" |
| Mar 2022 | Board | Asked staff to "explore options". No vote. |
| Aug 2023 | Legal | Answered the May 2021 question: yes, the City Manager has that authority. The memo went to the City Manager. Nothing followed. |
| Sep 2025 | Board | Eleven residents asked about it in public comment. The Chair said it is "with procurement". The board asked for a written update, and none is recorded. |

The Chair's statement in 2025 is out of date. Procurement can't fix this. It has been a City Manager decision since at least August 2023.

## What the closure costs

The 2026 budget carries these lines for keeping the bridge closed:
- PW-117 fencing rental: $18,400 a year
- PW-118 biennial inspection: $6,200, about $3,100 a year
- PK-033 signage: $900

That comes to about $21,500 a year for 2026. The disputed retention is $41,200, so roughly two years of closure costs already exceed it.

The folder has no budgets for earlier years. If fencing cost about the same from 2021 to 2026, the City has spent around $110k on fencing alone to avoid settling a $41k claim. **That figure is an estimate.** To confirm it, pull PW-117 actuals for FY2021–2025.

## What the folder doesn't say (check before relying on the plan above)

- **Whether the bridge would pass a load test today.** The repair was completed six years ago. The bridge has had biennial inspections (PW-118), but none of the reports are in this folder. Read the most recent one before promising a reopening date.
- **Whether Hallam still has its certification** and is willing to do the work after a five-year dispute. A phone call would answer this.
- **Whether another certified firm could do the test.** The list is described as "for our county". Nothing here says whether a firm certified in a neighbouring county or statewide could be used, or whether Policy 3.7 can be waived. Either would be a second route. Neither is needed if the claim is settled.
- **A simpler fix may exist.** Hallam could formally "submit" the drawing it already emailed and paint the rail. That would clear the punch list, release the retention, and end the claim without any settlement. It depends on both sides wanting to end this, and nothing in the folder suggests anyone has asked.

# Why the eggs fall

## Short answer

The fingers aren't the problem. The controller's force ceiling is.

The controller asks for `force_per_gram_n × mass` = 0.062 N/g × mass, then clamps it at
`force_ceiling_n` = 4.3 N. 4.3 / 0.062 = **69.35 g**. Any egg heavier than that gets less
grip force than the controller's own rule says it needs. In this log, every one of those eggs
that was more than 0.2 g over the line fell.

## The evidence (cycles.csv, 400 cycles, revs B/C/D)

| group | cycles | drops |
|---|---|---|
| commanded force below the 4.3 N ceiling | 387 | **0** |
| commanded force clamped at 4.3 N | 13 | **10** |

Here are all 13 clamped cycles, sorted by egg mass:

| mass (g) | force needed (N) | rev | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 69.4 | 4.30 | B | ok |
| 69.5 | 4.31 | C | ok |
| 69.5 | 4.31 | D | ok |
| 69.7 | 4.32 | D | drop |
| 69.9 | 4.33 | D | drop |
| 69.9 | 4.33 | D | drop |
| 70.0 | 4.34 | B | drop |
| 70.4 | 4.36 | C | drop |
| 70.5 | 4.37 | D | drop |
| 70.8 | 4.39 | D | drop |
| 71.3 | 4.42 | D | drop |
| 73.3 | 4.54 | B | drop |
| 76.6 | 4.75 | B | drop |

- The split is clean: eggs up to 69.5 g held, eggs from 69.7 g up fell. That's a single
  threshold. Nothing about it looks random.
- 10 drops in 400 cycles is 1 in 40, which matches the notes. 1 in 40 isn't a property of
  the fingers. It's roughly the share of eggs in this batch heavier than 69.4 g (13/400,
  about 1 in 31).
- Finger revision doesn't matter. B dropped 3 of 4 over-threshold eggs, C 1 of 2, D 6 of 7.
  D looks worse only because more heavy eggs went through the rig during D's run.
- Orientation (long/short) doesn't matter: drops happened in both.
- The actuator does what it's told. Measured force tracks commanded force within 0.04 N on
  every cycle, so the cause isn't the force loop or sensor drift.
- The slip column (`slip_ms`, 87–128 ms) has a value only on drop cycles, so the rig sees
  the slip. But `slip_detect` is `false` in config.json, so the controller never acts on it.

A side note: a shortfall of only 0.01–0.02 N decides whether an egg holds or drops. So
0.062 N/g is right at the friction limit, with no safety margin. Above the cap, any margin
the new pads added was too small to show up.

## What I'd tell the designer

1. **Don't machine rev E.** Three finger revisions already show the drop rate doesn't depend
   on the fingers. A cupped profile would hit the same 69.35 g wall.
2. **The ceiling is the cause.** It was added in 2025-11 after two crushed eggs at a trade
   show, and it set a mass limit no one wrote down. The rig's heaviest egg (76.6 g) needs
   4.75 N under the current gain. Large/jumbo eggs go higher still.
3. **Fix it on purpose, not by guessing.** The gripper needs a crush limit and a hold limit,
   and right now the two overlap. Before you change anything, measure what force actually
   crushes eggs on these pads. The trade-show note doesn't say what force did it, or whether
   the gain or pads were the same back then. Then choose:
   - raise the ceiling to somewhere between about 4.8 N and the measured crush force, if
     there's room; or
   - keep the ceiling and turn away or flag eggs over about 69 g (the mass is already known
     when the force is commanded, so this is a one-line check); or
   - turn on `slip_detect` and re-grip or ramp the force when slip starts, since the
     signal is already there 90–130 ms before the egg is lost.
4. **Add margin to the gain.** 0.062 N/g has none, so any extra friction from better pads
   is the cheapest margin available. The ceiling just has to allow for it.
5. **Check it:** run another 400 cycles with the change, deliberately including about 30
   eggs over 70 g. Expected result: 0 drops among them, and no crushes.

To harrow & pell. All numbers below come from `reports.csv` and `residents.csv`. `node analyze.js` reproduces them.

More than half of all reports (58 of 109) were filed by two accounts, **ledgerwick** and **quillon**. Both joined on 2026-07-22. Leave them out and report volume has not tripled. It went up for a few weeks while brassmoth was spamming, and it is now back to where it was in the first weeks.

| week | all | ledgerwick + quillon | everyone else |

| 5 | 24 | 13 | 11 |
| 6 | 20 | 12 | 8 |

| 8 | 16 | 12 | 4 |

- **Who they report.** Between them they reported 11 different people. Every one of them joined after 07-22. Of the 12 residents who joined after them, they reported 11. The one they skipped is brassmoth, the only newcomer whom everyone else *did* report. They have never reported anyone who was already in town. Nobody has ever reported them.
- **No one else agrees with them.** Their 58 reports have no corroboration at all: other residents filed 0 reports against any of their 11 targets. Compare brassmoth: 19 spam reports from 14 different residents, including both of you.
- **Their reasons are the ones that are hard to check.** All 58 are spam, bad faith or impersonation. They never file "off-topic" or "harassment", the reasons other residents use most.
- **Some reports came before the account existed.** By the `joined` column, kestrel-bot was reported 2 days before it joined, dorrit 5 days before, sedge 3 and tobiah 3. Either the join dates are wrong, or these accounts were reported before they could have posted anything. Check this first. It is the cheapest fact here to verify.
- **Duplicates.** quillon reported the same person twice on the same day four times (ines, mote, arlo, vela).

## What the proposed rule would have done

I simulated "3+ reports in one week → 48h mute", using both calendar weeks and a rolling 7-day window:

- **brassmoth**: muted. That one is correct: 14 independent reporters.
- **kestrel-bot, ines, papaver, dorrit, mote, arlo, tobiah, sedge, vela**: muted, many of them repeatedly (rolling window: vela on 5 separate days, arlo 4, mote 4). Take the pair's reports out and **none** of these would ever have crossed the threshold.

Two accounts working together can reach "3 reports" against anyone, as often as they like. The rule would hand them a button that mutes newcomers, and it would do it automatically. As far as this data shows, they are using it on newcomers already, by hand.

# Mill Creek footbridge: why it is still closed

## Short answer

The repair is finished. Hallam Structural replaced the corroded stringers on **2 November 2020**,
on schedule (Parks Board minutes, Nov 2020). For nearly six years the bridge has been closed
waiting for a **post-repair load test**, not a repair. That test has never been booked, because
three rules lock together and nobody with the power to unlock them has been asked to:

1. **Ordinance 14-212 §4** says the load test has to be done by a firm on the state certified list
   for pedestrian structures. In this county there is **one firm on that list: Hallam Structural.**
2. The City is holding back Hallam's **$41,200 retention** because of a closeout punch list. Hallam
   has filed a claim for the money.
3. **City Policy 3.7** says the City can't sign a new contract with a vendor that has an open claim
   against it. So the only firm allowed to do the test is the one firm the City isn't allowed to hire.

The punch list has two cosmetic items: touch-up paint on the north rail, and an as-built drawing.
Hallam emailed the drawing, but the contract says "submitted". The legal dispute comes down to
whether emailing counts as submitting (engineering email, May 2021).

## The key that already exists

In August 2023 Legal told the City Manager in writing that the **City Manager can settle the Hallam
claim alone, under the $50,000 delegated authority in Admin Code 2.40.** The claim is $41,200, which
is under that limit. Settling closes the claim, and that lifts the Policy 3.7 bar. Legal adds: "No
action has been requested from this office since."

Since then:
- In March 2022 the Board asked staff to "explore options". It took no vote.
- In September 2025 the Chair told eleven residents the matter was "with procurement". Procurement
  can't fix it, because it is the office that applies Policy 3.7. The Board asked for a written
  update, and no update appears in later minutes.

No document shows the Board, Procurement or Engineering asking the City Manager to use that
authority. Each office describes the lock correctly, and each one points at another office.

## What the closure is costing

From the 2026 budget excerpt:

| Line | Item | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| PW-117 | Fencing rental (annual) | $18,400 / yr |
| PW-118 | Inspection (biennial) | $6,200 every 2 yrs |
| PK-033 | Sign: "Bridge closed for repairs" | $900 |

If the fencing has cost about the same each year since 2020 (I only have the 2026 figure), six years
of fencing comes to about **$110,000**. That is roughly 2.7 times the $41,200 in dispute, before
counting inspections. The City keeps paying every year to avoid paying a one-time amount it has
already agreed it owes, apart from one drawing. The sign is also wrong: the repairs ended in 2020.

## What would actually reopen it

**Step 1: settle the claim.** The City Manager uses Admin Code 2.40 to settle the Hallam retention
claim. Two ways to do it:
- Release the $41,200, and treat the paint touch-up as a small deduction or a warranty item. Or:
- Have Hallam formally submit the as-built drawing it has already emailed, then release the money.
  This would satisfy the "submitted" wording at no real cost to either side.

This step needs one decision from one person, and Legal has already said that person has the
authority. A written request from the Parks Board Chair or the Public Works director to the City
Manager, citing the August 2023 legal memo, is the missing step.

**Step 2: book the load test.** Once the claim is closed, Policy 3.7 no longer applies. Procurement
contracts Hallam for the load test under Ord. 14-212 §4.

**Step 3: pass the test and reopen.** Then remove the fencing (PW-117) and the sign.

## Stopping the same lock next time

The same lock will come back the next time the only certified firm has a dispute with the City.
Two rule changes would prevent it:
- **Amend Policy 3.7** to add an exception for when the vendor is the only state-certified provider
  of a legally required safety service. The exception could need City Manager or Board approval.
- **Let a certified firm from a neighboring county count** for §4 tests, or ask the state to certify
  more firms in this county.

A further point for the Board: right now Hallam would be load-testing its own repair. Whatever
happens with the claim, the Board should ask whether §4 was meant to require an independent tester.
That is another reason to allow more than one firm.

## What the folder doesn't tell me

- Whether Hallam still exists and is still on the certified list in 2026, or would take the work.
- Whether the claim is still open, or has lapsed, been decided, or been withdrawn.
- What the load test costs.
- Whether anyone ever sent the City Manager the 2023 memo as a request for action. The memo exists,
  but no reply appears.

Each of these can be checked with one phone call before Step 1. None of them changes the order of
the steps.

# Why the eggs fall

## Short answer

The fingers aren't dropping the eggs. The controller's force ceiling is.

`config.json` sets grip force as `0.062 N/g × egg mass`, then caps it at `force_ceiling_n: 4.3`.
The cap starts to bind at **4.3 / 0.062 ≈ 69.4 g**. Any egg heavier than that gets less force
than the controller's own rule says it needs. In this log, those are the eggs that fall.

## Evidence (all 400 cycles in `cycles.csv`)

| | cycles | drops |
|---|---|---|
| egg ≤ 69.35 g (force not capped) | 387 | **0** |
| egg > 69.35 g (force capped at 4.30 N) | 13 | **10** |

- **Every one of the 10 drops** is an egg of 69.7–76.6 g with `force_cmd_n` pinned at exactly 4.30.
- The 3 capped eggs that held were 69.4–69.5 g. Their force shortfall was under 0.01 N, so they were capped in name only.
- 20 eggs between 67 and 69.3 g all held, with no slip at all. Nothing gets worse gradually as eggs get heavier. Below the cap there's no problem, and above it there is.
- The actuator does what it's told. Measured force tracks commanded force to within 0.04 N on every cycle. The force is short because of the command, not the hardware.
- `slip_ms` is only recorded on drops (87–128 ms of slip before the egg let go). There's no slip on any cycle that held.
- Orientation and `close_mm` don't separate drops from successes. Drops happen in both orientations and across the normal close range.

### Why each finger revision seemed to fail the same way, and why D looked *worse*

| rev | cycles | eggs over the cap | drops |
|---|---|---|---|
| B | 130 | 4 | 3 |
| C | 140 | 2 | 1 |
| D | 130 | 7 | 6 |

Each revision's drop count is almost exactly its count of over-cap eggs. Rev D's "worse" rate
comes from that batch of eggs having more heavy ones. It says nothing about the wider contact
patch or the +0.4 mm offset. The roughly 1-in-40 rate is just how often an egg over 69.4 g turns
up in the supply. Pads, texture and geometry changed three times, and none of them changed that.

## What I'd tell the designer

1. **Don't machine rev E yet.** A cupped profile might hide the problem by adding mechanical
   retention. But it would be a fourth set of fingers built to work around one line of config.
2. **The ceiling has a history, so revisit it rather than just deleting it.** The note says it went
   in in 2025-11 "after two crushed eggs at the trade show demo." It's a fix for one failure that
   created another. Before raising it, find out what actually crushed those eggs. At 0.062 N/g, the
   heaviest egg here only asks for 4.75 N. Static crush loads for eggs are usually reported in the
   tens of newtons (check this on your own rig). That makes me suspect the demo crushes came from
   something else, like closing impact at 12 mm/s, overshoot, or a bad mass reading, and not from
   steady grip force. The cap may have been put on the wrong variable.
3. **Concrete change to test:** raise `force_ceiling_n` to at least about 5.0 N. That covers the
   76.6 g egg (4.75 N) with some margin. Then rerun a batch weighted toward heavy eggs (70–78 g)
   and confirm drops go to zero and nothing cracks. If crushing really is a risk near 5 N, the
   answer is to stop gripping eggs above about 69 g, not to grip them too lightly.
4. **Turn on `slip_detect`.** The rig already measures slip, and every drop slipped for about
   90–130 ms before falling. That's enough time for a controller to add force. Right now the
   gripper sees the egg going and does nothing.
5. **Log one more column:** whether the ceiling clamped on that cycle. If that flag had been there
   in June, this would have shown up after the first drop instead of after three finger
   revisions.

## Caveat

Ten drops is a small sample. But the split is perfectly clean: 0 drops in 387 uncapped cycles and
10 in 13 capped ones. That's strong enough to justify a config test before any more machining. If
heavy eggs at about 5 N still drop, then look at the fingers again.

A reviewer says that is implausibly good for their instrument and has asked them to check the data reduction against the method the paper states. The folder you're in is their pipeline, its tests, the published method (README.md) and three sessions of raw data. The reviewer is right. The pipeline did not do what the paper's method says, and the ±0.02‰ came from those errors, not from the instrument.

**What was wrong.** The ratio and drift-correction steps matched the stated method. The uncertainty steps had four mistakes:
- **Standard error divided by n instead of √n.** This alone made the errors about 6 times too small.
- **Outliers rejected at 2 standard deviations, not 3.**
- **Rejection repeated** until nothing more was dropped, instead of done once.
- **Population standard deviation** used instead of the sample one (n − 1). This only matters by about 1%.

The data files themselves are clean, so the problem was entirely in the code.

**Corrected results.** Done the way the paper says, the standard errors are **0.064, 0.082 and 0.064‰** for s01, s02 and s03, against 0.008–0.009‰ from the old code. **What I changed.** I fixed `lib/stats.mjs` and `lib/reduce.mjs`, and added tests in `test.mjs` that would have caught each mistake; they all pass. The original tests only checked the mean, the line fit and a flat standard. `REVIEW.md` has the reply, with a before/after table for each session.

One caveat, which the reply also states: even the corrected standard error leaves out the uncertainty of the drift line fitted through the standards. The real uncertainty is therefore a bit larger again. I didn't add that term, because the paper's method doesn't include it.

# Response to reviewer: precision of reported δ values

The reviewer is right. We checked the reduction code against the method stated in the paper,
and it did not do what the paper says. The ±0.02‰ figure comes from those errors. With the
reduction corrected, the standard errors are 0.064–0.082‰, about 7–9 times larger than what
the pipeline produced (0.008–0.009‰) and 3–4 times larger than the ±0.02‰ in the paper.

## What was wrong

Steps 1 and 2 (ratios, linear drift correction against the standards) matched the stated method.
Steps 3 and 4 did not:

| Stated method | What the code did | Effect on SE |
|---|---|---|
| SE = s / √n | SE = s / **n** | understated by a factor √n ≈ 6 (n = 32–42) |
| reject at **3** SD | rejected at **2** SD | trims real scatter, shrinks s |
| reject **once** | **iterated** until nothing more was rejected | removed 4–8 cycles per session, shrinks s further |
| sample SD (n − 1) | population SD (n) | ~1–2% low |

The SE divisor accounts for most of the error. The outlier rule mattered too. It discarded 8 of
40 sample cycles in s02, and it moved the session means by 0.06–0.08‰, which is about one
corrected standard error.

All three data files were checked: no malformed rows, no missing values, and times are in
order. The problem was in the code, not the data.

## Corrected results

Reduced exactly as stated in the Method section: drift-corrected δ, one pass of 3σ rejection
with the sample SD, and SE = s/√n.

| Session | n kept / sample cycles | δ (‰), as submitted | δ (‰), corrected | SE (‰), as submitted | SE (‰), corrected |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| s01 | 36 → **38** / 40 | −1.915 | **−1.858** | 0.0087 | **0.065** |
| s02 | 32 → **38** / 40 | 2.604 | **2.681** | 0.0091 | **0.082** |
| s03 | 42 → **46** / 48 | 0.295 | **0.378** | 0.0083 | **0.064** |

The 3σ rule now rejects two cycles per session: s01 at δ = −4.77 and +1.12‰, s02 at +0.23 and
+5.06‰, and s03 at −1.98 and +2.85‰. The cycle-level SD after rejection is 0.40–0.50‰. That is
consistent with the reviewer's expectation for a single-collector instrument.

We will revise the reported uncertainties to the corrected values (±0.07–0.08‰ at 1 SE). We
will also re-examine every conclusion that depended on differences between samples smaller than
about 0.2‰.

## Changes to the pipeline

- `lib/stats.mjs`: `sd` now divides by n − 1, and `stderr` now divides by √n.
- `lib/reduce.mjs`: `clean` makes a single pass at k = 3.
- `test.mjs`: new tests for the sample SD, SE = s/√n, drift correction against a sloped
  standard line, the 3σ threshold (a point at 2.2σ is kept and one at 4.25σ is rejected), the
  single pass (a point that a second pass would remove is kept), and an end-to-end reduction of
  a synthetic session. The original tests covered only the mean, the line fit and a flat

  repeatedly, usually in their first week or two, which is when a newcomer decides whether to stay.

to say whether ledgerwick and quillon were ever right. Please add an outcome column. Then you can
weight each reporter by their track record, and the next rule can be judged against what actually
happened.

- **Standard deviation:** the code divided by n instead of n − 1. This made it about 1% too small.
- **Outlier rejection:** the paper says one pass at 3 standard deviations. The code made repeated passes at 2 standard deviations until nothing more was removed. | s01 | −1.915 | 0.009 | −1.858 | 0.065 |

| s03 | +0.295 | 0.008 | +0.378 | 0.064 |

# Response to the reviewer: precision of the reported δ values

We thank the reviewer. **The reviewer is right.** The ±0.02‰ uncertainties in the manuscript
are wrong. They do not come from the instrument. They come from three errors in our
data-reduction code, and each error makes the code depart from the method as stated in the
paper. We have corrected the code to match the published method and re-reduced all three
sessions. The corrected standard errors are 0.064–0.082‰, about 7–9 times larger than the
values we reported. The δ values also change, by 0.06–0.08‰.

## What the code did, compared with what the paper says

| Step | Published method | What the code actually did | Effect on the reported SE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard error (step 4) | s / √n | s / **n** | Too small by a factor of √n (≈ 6–7 for our n) |
| Standard deviation (steps 3, 4) | sample SD, n − 1 | population SD, **n** | Slightly too small (≈ 1.3 %) |
| Outlier rejection (step 3) | **one pass at 3 SD** | repeated passes at **2 SD** until nothing more was removed | Removed real scatter: s01 lost 4 cycles, s02 lost 8, s03 lost 6. This shrank the SD and moved the mean |

The first error is the largest. Dividing by n instead of √n alone makes a ~0.06‰ standard
error look like ~0.01‰. The iterated 2σ clipping made it worse, because it kept trimming the
tails of a distribution that was not contaminated. Each pass removed good data and narrowed
the SD further. That is why sessions s02 and s03 lost far more cycles than one 3σ pass would
justify. The drift correction (step 2) and the ratio (step 1) were implemented as stated. We
checked them against an independent re-implementation.

## Corrected results

All values are in ‰. "As submitted" is the output of the uncorrected pipeline, which gave the
numbers in the manuscript.

| Session | As submitted: n | δ | SE | Corrected: n | δ | SE | Sample SD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| s01 | 36 | −1.9146 | 0.0087 | 38 / 40 | −1.8580 | 0.0650 | 0.401 |
| s02 | 32 | +2.6042 | 0.0091 | 38 / 40 | +2.6808 | 0.0818 | 0.504 |
| s03 | 42 | +0.2946 | 0.0083 | 46 / 48 | +0.3777 | 0.0642 | 0.435 |

With the stated method, a single 3σ pass rejects two cycles per session. In every session
these are the most extreme high value and the most extreme low value. The corrected per-cycle
scatter of ≈ 0.4–0.5‰ is consistent with a single-collector instrument. A standard error of
≈ 0.07‰ over ~40 cycles is what that scatter supports.

The shifts in δ (+0.057, +0.077, +0.083‰) are larger than the uncertainties we originally
claimed. For s03 the shift is also larger than the corrected SE. Any conclusion in the
manuscript that depends on differences between samples at the ≲ 0.2‰ level must be
re-examined with the corrected values and uncertainties. We will revise the text, tables and
figures accordingly. For the precision statement we will quote ±0.06–0.08‰ (1 SE) per sample.

## What we changed

- `lib/stats.mjs`: `sd` now divides by n − 1, and `stderr` now divides by √n.
- `lib/reduce.mjs`: `clean` now makes one pass at k = 3 and does not iterate.
- `test.mjs`: new tests pin each of these behaviours: the n − 1 SD, the √n standard error, the
  single non-iterated pass, and the 3σ (not 2σ) threshold. The original tests covered only the
  mean, the line fit and the drift-corrected δ. None of them exercised the uncertainty
  calculation, which is how these errors got through.
- We reproduced the corrected numbers with a second implementation written directly from the
  method text (closed-form least squares, separate statistics). It agrees to ~1e-12‰.

We checked the raw session files. All rows are complete, times are in order, and every cycle is
labelled `std` or `sample`. Nothing in the data contributed to the problem.

## Remaining caveat

Our standard error treats the sample cycles as independent. It does not include the
uncertainty of the drift line fitted through the standards. That uncertainty is common to all
sample cycles in a session, so averaging does not reduce it. The published method does not
include this term, and we have not added it. Adding it would increase the uncertainties
further, though modestly. If the reviewer considers it necessary, we will add it and state it
in the method.

# Wait-time dashboard: what the numbers show since the tablet

**The dashboard was wrong, and it's fixed now.** It had been dropping everyone who left without being
seen, so "walkouts" always read 0. It also started weeks on Sunday instead of Monday and picked the
wrong middle value for the median. The table below is the corrected version.

| Week of | Signed in | Seen | Left unseen | Median wait (min) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 23 Feb | 37 | 36 | 1 | 17 |
| 2 Mar | 44 | 42 | 2 | 16.5 |
| 9 Mar | 37 | 36 | 1 | 22 |
| **16 Mar (tablet starts)** | 37 | 33 | 4 | 31 |
| 23 Mar | 43 | 39 | 4 | 33 |
| 30 Mar | 33 | 29 | 4 | 39 |

**What changed on 16 March.** Daily patient numbers stayed about the same: 118 visits in the three paper
weeks, 113 in the three tablet weeks. But recorded waits roughly **doubled**, and they doubled on the first
tablet day. They did not creep up over time.

- On paper, a typical wait was 11–24 minutes and the middle one was 17. On the tablet it's 23–45
  minutes, with a middle of 34. ("Typical" here means the middle half of patients.)
- On paper, 39 of 114 waits were under 14 minutes. On the tablet, none of 101 are. Every tablet day's
  shortest wait is 14 minutes or more.
- The week of 9 March was a little higher on paper (22). That is mostly one slow day, 10 March. It
  isn't the start of a trend.

**People leaving unseen went from 4 (of 118) to 12 (of 113).** If nothing had really changed, a gap
this big would turn up by luck only about 1 time in 25. So it's probably real, but not certain. It
isn't double sign-ins: most of those 12 had nobody else sign in within 10 minutes of them.

**One thing only you can answer:** on Wed 25 March and Fri 27 March the last tablet sign-in is at
exactly 11:59, after a normal morning (10 and 6 patients). On Thu 2 April it's the reverse: the first
sign-in is at 11:53, and there were only 5 patients all day. Was the clinic closed those half-days? If
it wasn't, the tablet lost sign-ins around midday, and that belongs in the call to the vendor.

**What we can't tell you yet: is the tablet measuring differently, or are people really waiting longer?**
Probably some of both. A jump that big on day one, with no short waits at all afterwards, looks like the
tablet starting or stopping the clock at a different moment than the paper sheet did. For example, "seen"
might now get pressed at rooming or checkout instead of when the patient is called. The extra walkouts
point the other way, toward people really waiting longer. But they aren't clean evidence either. On the
tablet, "left unseen" just means nobody pressed "seen", so a forgotten press counts as a walkout.

**Three checks, cheapest first:**
1. Ask the tablet vendor, or whoever set it up, exactly what records "signed in" and "seen". One phone
   call, and probably the answer to most of this. Ask too whether it can drop or delay entries.
2. Compare the tablet's clock to a phone.
3. Spend one morning in the waiting room yourself. Time about 10 patients from sign-in to being called,
   and note anyone who actually leaves. Compare against what the tablet records for them.

We don't suggest having the front desk keep a paper log alongside the tablet. It adds work, and it asks
the people being measured to produce the measurement.

**Until then:** don't compare tablet waits with paper waits. They may not be measuring the same thing.
If you want one number to watch, watch people leaving unseen, and keep in mind that it can be inflated
by missed button presses. If the tablet allows it, a separate "left without being seen" button would
stop a forgotten press from counting as a walkout.

# rota — the clinic shift rota

    node cli.mjs people.json 2026-11-02 28

prints the rota as JSON, one key per date, each a list of two names:

    {"2026-11-02":["Ana","Bea"],"2026-11-03":[...], ...}

It must follow POLICY.md. It exits non-zero with a message on stderr if no rota can be made.
Every policy rule is a hard constraint: if the rules can't all hold for a team and period (for
example, too few nurse shifts inside the fair-share bounds to put a nurse on every day), it
refuses rather than bending one. The decision about which rule gives way belongs to the clinic.
The message names the days and the rules that clash. One rule of thumb follows from rules 1 and 4:
over long periods the policy can only hold if the nurses' total fte (after leave) is at least the
aides', because a nurse every day means the aides can fill at most half the shifts.
The policy judges each period on its own. Ties between people equally due a shift go by an order
drawn from the start date, not by the team file's (alphabetical) order. That alone is not enough:
a share like "1.5 weekend shifts" gets rounded the same way nearly every time, so the same person
gains or loses half a shift every rota, all of it legal. To stop that, pass the earlier rotas:

    node cli.mjs people.json 2026-11-30 28 rota-2026-11-02.json [older rotas ...]

The new rota then leans toward whoever is owed, still inside the policy's bounds (a rota never
changes legality because of history). For the clinic's team over 5 years of 4-week rotas, nobody
drifts more than 1.1 shifts or 0.6 weekend shifts from their share overall. Without the earlier
rotas, Dov ends 21.6 weekend shifts short (or 32.5 over, when periods start on a Saturday).
Keep old leave dates in people.json; the shares of past periods are worked out from it.
`node test.mjs` runs the tests. Code: `lib/people.mjs` (load and validate the team),
`lib/calendar.mjs` (dates), `lib/assign.mjs` (who works when), `cli.mjs`.
